Summary: Trade Database (Postgres)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A normalised Postgres schema is the transactional record of what a customer asked for and what happened next. \\ * Accounts, instruments, orders and positions are modelled from the domain, version controlled as migrations, and rebuildable from the files alone. \\ * Constraints, indexes, historical trade structures, an ER diagram and seed data are in place, and every team member can walk the model unaided. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Nothing is handed over. There is no transactional schema in contracts/, because the modelling is the assessment. Read sprint-03-trade-database/README.md for the domain. \\ * Read contracts/trade-api.yaml while you design. It is the contract the Sprint 6 service satisfies out of this database, and a schema that cannot serve it is the wrong schema. \\ * The analytical store is a separate concern. contracts/analytics-schema.sql is read in Sprint 4 and loaded in Sprint 7. It is ANSI SQL and runs on Snowflake, DuckDB or SQLite. \\ * Security focus: parameterised access from Sprint 6 onwards (OWASP A03), domain rules enforced by constraints rather than hoped for in application code, least-privilege database roles, no credentials in connection config. \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-03-trade-database/scripts/check.sh.

Summary: Conceptual Data Model and ER Diagram
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Entities, attributes, keys, cardinality and optionality are identified from the domain brief rather than copied from a table list. \\ * One ER diagram is committed under design/ and every member of the team can walk the whole of it unaided. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Identify the entities the domain requires: accounts, instruments, orders and positions, and the relationships between them. \\ Decide the cardinality and optionality of every relationship and be ready to say where each came from. \\ Commit the diagram as Mermaid in design/er-diagram.md, or as an exported image in design/. Commit the export, not a link to a cloud document. \\ Commit a short data dictionary alongside it. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Mermaid is the better choice: it diffs in review and it cannot drift out of the repository. \\ * The review walks the diagram against the migrations. Update it when the schema moves.

Summary: Normalisation to Third Normal Form
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The schema is in third normal form with no redundant or transitive dependencies. \\ * Any deliberate denormalisation is documented with the reason for it. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Work the model through first, second and third normal form and record what moved at each step. \\ Write the normalisation notes into design/ so the reasoning can be reviewed rather than inferred. \\ Where you denormalise on purpose, name the query that justifies it and the write cost you accepted.

Summary: Entities, Lifecycles and Constraints as Migrations
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Numbered migration files under migrations/ create the schema, apply in filename order, and rebuild the database from the files alone. \\ * Foreign keys and check constraints enforce the domain rules, including at least three check constraints, one of them covering account state. \\ * Money is represented exactly, never as binary floating point. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Model the account lifecycle so that ACTIVE trades, SUSPENDED can be read and cannot trade, and CLOSED never trades again and is never deleted. \\ Model the order lifecycle so that an order starts at NEW and reaches exactly one terminal state of FILLED, REJECTED or CANCELLED, and rejected orders are retained. \\ Model an instrument that can stop being tradable without ceasing to exist, so that old orders still resolve and new ones are refused. \\ Give the account row a way for a second concurrent writer to discover that it lost rather than overwriting the first. \\ Choose exact numeric types for cash balances and prices and apply them consistently. \\ Number migrations from 001_ and treat an applied migration as immutable once the design review has happened. Change the schema by adding 002_, 003_ and so on. \\ Copy the migration and seed files into infra/postgres/ so a fresh docker compose up -d builds the database unattended from Sprint 6. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Apply everything with sprint-03-trade-database/scripts/apply.sh, and --fresh to wipe and rebuild. Run it often. A schema that only works because of something a teammate typed into psql on Tuesday will not survive the showcase. \\ * Positions are derived state and are stored anyway, because the dashboard cannot replay an order history on every page load. Be able to demonstrate the reconciliation.

Summary: Idempotency Key Enforced by the Database
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A unique constraint covers the order idempotency key, and a duplicate insert is refused by the database. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Carry a client-generated idempotency key on every order and make it unique across all orders forever. \\ Enforce the uniqueness with a database constraint rather than a read followed by an insert. \\ Write probes/duplicate-idempotency-key.sql so that it inserts one valid order twice with the same key. The harness expects the second insert to fail with SQLSTATE 23505. \\ Write probes/orphan-foreign-key.sql so that it inserts one row referencing a parent that does not exist. The harness expects SQLSTATE 23503. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Read then insert is not enforcement. Two concurrent requests both read nothing and both insert, and the customer has bought twice. \\ * Sprint 6 depends on that failure being detectable, and Sprint 7 depends on it again from a different process. Design for it now.

Summary: Indexes Justified Against the Named Queries
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * At least three indexes exist that are not primary key or constraint indexes, and each is justified by one of the seven named queries. \\ * The justifications are committed in design/indexes.md. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Write the seven queries in the brief as SQL and run them against your seeded database. \\ Read the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after adding each index. \\ Write a justification that names the query, states what the plan does with and without the index, and says what the index costs on write. \\ Where a key you already declared serves a query with no new index, write that down with the plan that proves it. It is a real finding and it does not count towards the three. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * An index is paid for on every insert and every update to the columns it covers, and orders is the most write-heavy table you have. No index goes in without a query behind it. \\ * It seemed likely to help is not a justification.

Summary: Historical Trade Data Structures
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Structures retaining the detail of what was executed, when and at what achieved price exist alongside the operational tables. \\ * How they are populated and how they are queried is documented. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Design structures the Sprint 7 extract can pull incrementally, without scanning the whole history every night. \\ Document the population path and the query path in design/. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * This is the operational side of the boundary. The analytical star schema in contracts/analytics-schema.sql is the other side, and it is loaded in Sprint 7. \\ * The decision to record, and the reason for it, matters more than the volume of rows you load.

Summary: Seed Data
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Seed data loads with one command after the migrations and covers active, suspended and closed accounts. \\ * Every one of the seven named queries returns something against the seeded database. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Seed accounts in all three states, including one with a balance too small to afford a realistic order. \\ Seed several instruments, including at least one that is not an equity and at least one that is no longer tradable. \\ Seed orders spanning more than one lifecycle state, including at least one that was rejected. \\ Seed holdings on more than one account, consistent with the filled orders that produced them. \\ Use symbols the Fauxnance API actually serves, so quotes resolve in Sprint 7 without a second pass over your fixtures. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Sprint 4 and Sprint 7 both read this data. Thin seed data is a fortnight of friction later.

Summary: Manifest, Probes and the Acceptance Harness
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * manifest.env declares the names the harness needs and sprint-03-trade-database/scripts/check.sh passes from a clean state. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Fill in manifest.env once the first migration exists: the accounts table, its state column and the three literal values it stores, the orders table and the idempotency key column. \\ Run scripts/check.sh and read what it asserts. It builds a scratch database, applies every migration and seed file to it, runs its assertions and drops it. Your working database is never touched. \\ Fix what it names and rerun until clean. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The harness never asserts a name it was not given and has no opinion about the rest of your schema. \\ * Passing is necessary and not sufficient. It cannot tell you whether the schema is in third normal form, whether an index is justified or merely present, or whether your team can explain any of it. The design review is the assessment.

Summary: Analytics and the Ingestion Pipeline (Python)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A Python dashboard states at least three business claims, each supported by a chart a non-technical reader can read unaided. \\ * Ingestion is structured as three separable extract, transform and load functions, with pytest over at least the transform. \\ * Market data is pulled from the Fauxnance API with the key read from the environment, and rate limits and errors are handled by class rather than by a bare try block. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The source this week is market data because the platform has no order flow yet. In Sprint 7 the same three functions are pointed at the platform's own trades and load the star schema. Build it as though the source were going to change, because it is. \\ * contracts/analytics-schema.sql is the analytical model. It is plain ANSI SQL and runs unchanged on Snowflake, DuckDB or SQLite. What is assessed is the model and the load, not the vendor. \\ * Fauxnance serves end-of-day candles and delayed quotes over HTTP. There is no stream, and the quota is 2000 requests per day per key. \\ * Security focus: validation and data-quality decisions (OWASP A08), safe handling of financial data, and a key that never reaches the repository. \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-04-analytics-etl/scripts/check.sh.

Summary: Fauxnance Client with the Key from the Environment
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Historical candles are pulled through GET /candles/{symbol} with the key read from FAUXNANCE_API_KEY and from nowhere else. \\ * Raw pulls are cached to disk so that a re-run costs nothing against the quota. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Build the client under src/analytics/fauxnance/, sending the key in the X-Api-Key header. \\ Copy .env.example at the repository root to .env, which is git-ignored, and put your key there. \\ Cache the raw response under .cache/ keyed by symbol and range, and read it back when it is already there. \\ Check GET /usage before assuming the API is broken, and GET /health, which needs no key, before assuming anything at all. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Cache the raw response, not the cleaned frame. Changing the transform is the thing you will do most this week and it should not need a fresh pull. \\ * The key is never a literal in source, never in a test, never in a fixture, never in a notebook you commit. A key that reaches a commit has to be revoked, and the history keeps it whether or not you revoke it.

Summary: Error Handling by Failure Class
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Rate-limit and error handling is present and distinguishes the four failure classes, and is not a bare try block. \\ * A teammate can tell from the logs which of the four happened without rerunning the pipeline. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Handle an exhausted quota: HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Stop and say so plainly. Sleeping until midnight inside a batch run is not recovery. \\ Handle a request that is wrong: another 4xx. Fail that symbol, keep the message and carry on with the others, because retrying repeats the mistake. \\ Handle nothing reaching the service: a connection error or timeout. Retry with a growing backoff and give up after a small number of attempts. \\ Handle a response that arrived and is wrong: HTTP 200 carrying a bad row. That belongs to the transform, which decides between dropping, quarantining and raising. \\ Never log the key.

Summary: Extract, Transform and Load as Three Separable Functions
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The pipeline is three functions in three modules, wired by a fourth that does nothing else, and each is individually callable. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Write extract so that it obtains raw responses and hands them on unchanged. It is the only part that needs a key and a network. \\ Write transform so that it takes data and returns data. It opens no socket, reads no environment variable and writes nowhere. \\ Write load so that it writes the result into the analytical store, and make it the only part that writes. \\ Declare the three as module:function entries in manifest.env. \\ Give the pipeline an entry point a teammate can run without reading the source, and say which in a note at the bottom of claims.md. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A pipeline that fetches, cleans and writes in one function can only be tested against the live API, and when it produces a wrong number there is no way to ask which third of it was wrong.

Summary: Three Business Claims
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * claims.md holds at least three claims, each stated as a sentence about the business that could turn out to be wrong, and each naming the chart artefact that supports it. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ State what is true, of what, over what period and by how much, so that a reader could disagree and checking the data would settle it. \\ Name the artefact behind each claim, using a fragment where one file holds several charts. \\ Be ready to trace the numbers behind one claim back to the rows they came from. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A chart description is not a claim. It tells the reader what the picture is of and leaves them to work out whether anything follows. \\ * Be ready to answer what would have to be true for this claim to be wrong.

Summary: Charts a Non-Technical Reader Can Read Unaided
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Each claim is supported by a committed chart artefact that opens with no network and no build step. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Choose the chart type that fits each claim and write it out under src/analytics/dashboard/. \\ Label both axes with units, and title the chart with the finding rather than the variable names. \\ Remove unexplained abbreviations, tickers without a company name, and legend entries that only make sense to whoever wrote the query. \\ Commit the artefacts at the paths named in claims.md. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A dashboard that only exists while a notebook kernel is running cannot be assessed, and a chart that loads its library from a content delivery network is a blank page on a locked-down machine. \\ * The reader has your chart and no access to you.

Summary: pytest over the Transform, Including the Malformed Case
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * pytest covers at least the transform step and includes at least one malformed-input case, and the suite never touches the network. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Use the canned responses in fixtures/, loaded by tests/conftest.py, one of which is deliberately corrupted. \\ Read fixtures/README.md, decide what your transform does with each defect it lists, then assert it. \\ Declare the malformed-input test in manifest.env as a pytest node id so the harness can run it on its own. \\ Delete tests/test_example_fixture_use.py once your own tests use the fixtures. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a valid payload transforms to the expected frame \\ # a row missing a required field is handled as your transform declares \\ # a row whose high is below its low is refused rather than loaded \\ # an empty response is handled without error \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Dropping a row, quarantining it and raising are all defensible, and they are not equally defensible for all of the defects. \\ * A suite that needs the API to be up fails on a train and gets skipped by the third person who sees it fail.

Summary: Read the Analytical Star Schema
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The team can explain the star in contracts/analytics-schema.sql: one fact table, its three dimensions, the grain, and why the analytical store is separate from the operational one. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read the description block at the top of contracts/analytics-schema.sql, including the portability rules and the loading notes. \\ Stand the schema up on your chosen target and load it with something small, so the shape is familiar before Sprint 7 loads it for real. \\ Record which target your team is using and why. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The schema is given because it is a modelling style you have not met yet, and because two teams inventing incompatible fact tables would make the Sprint 7 pipeline work unassessable. \\ * Snowflake is the target named in the curriculum. DuckDB is the recommended default when Snowflake is unavailable and costs no marks. SQLite is acceptable with its typing limitation stated.

Summary: Manifest, Packaging and the Acceptance Harness
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The package installs into an empty environment and sprint-04-analytics-etl/scripts/check.sh passes. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Fill in manifest.env: the three pipeline functions and the malformed-input test node id. \\ Run scripts/check.sh, which builds a scratch virtual environment, installs the package into it and runs your suite there. It needs no database and never calls Fauxnance. \\ Fix what it names and rerun until clean. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The harness runs your malformed-input test, it does not read it. A test that asserts nothing passes here. It measures the length of a claim, not its truth, and it has never opened one of your charts.

Summary: Trading Domain Engine (Java and OOAD)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The trading rules live in a plain Java 21 library with no Spring, no servlet API and no JDBC driver anywhere in the dependency tree. \\ * Entities, the three enumerations, a validated request DTO, an exception hierarchy over the six specified cases and business rules 1 to 8 are implemented in the domain. \\ * Tests are written before implementation and the fact is evidenced in the commit history. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Two callers read these rules. Sprint 6 wraps them in a Spring Boot controller and Sprint 7 calls them again from a Kafka consumer, in a different process, against a price that did not exist when the order was placed. A rule that leaked into a controller has to be written twice, and the two copies drift. \\ * Nothing here starts a container, opens a socket or reads an environment variable, and it should stay that way. \\ * Security focus: validation in the domain model, defensive coding, and error messages that carry no internal detail (OWASP A05). \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-05-domain-engine/scripts/check.sh.

Summary: UML Class and Sequence Diagrams
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A class diagram of the domain and a sequence diagram of order placement are committed under design/ and match the code. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Draw every type you wrote, its fields, the operations that carry behaviour, the enumerations, the exception hierarchy and the relationships with their cardinality. \\ Draw one order arriving at the domain and the eight rules being evaluated in order, showing what is consulted at each step and where each failure leaves the flow. \\ Draw the refusal paths, not only the happy path. \\ Commit as Mermaid in design/class-diagram.md and design/sequence-diagram.md, or as an exported image. \\ Update the diagrams when the code moves. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The review walks the diagram against the code. An assessor picks a class off the diagram, opens it, and expects the fields, operations and relationships to match. Every team member walks the whole diagram, including the parts they did not write.

Summary: Domain Entities
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Account, Instrument, Order and Position are implemented and match the domain model. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Give Account the behaviour that moves its own balance, and refuse a debit that would leave it negative before anything is subtracted. \\ Keep both account identifiers on Account and keep them distinguishable: the numeric key that the platform passes around, and the customer-facing reference quoted on a support call. \\ Have Account report the version it was loaded at, for the optimistic lock Sprint 6 applies. The domain does not take the lock. \\ Give Instrument the symbol as its natural key and let it answer whether it may be traded, which is business rule 3. \\ Give Order both prices and keep them apart: the limit price the customer submitted, and the executed price the Trade Executor achieves in Sprint 7, which does not exist until the order is filled. \\ Have Order refuse a transition that is not allowed, rather than leaving that to whoever called it. \\ Give Position the asymmetric average cost rule: a buy recalculates the average across the old holding and the new units, a sell reduces the quantity and leaves the average cost alone. \\ Represent money as a decimal at two decimal places and never as a double. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Keeping the cost basis intact through a sale is what makes realised profit and loss computable at the point of sale, and the Sprint 10 Portfolio extension depends on it. \\ * Short selling is out of scope, so a position never goes negative.

Summary: The Three Enumerations, Exactly
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * AccountStatus holds exactly ACTIVE, SUSPENDED and CLOSED. OrderSide holds exactly BUY and SELL. OrderStatus holds exactly NEW, FILLED, REJECTED and CANCELLED. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Declare the three enumerations under your base package with no extra and no renamed literal. \\ Spell CANCELLED with two Ls. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * These literals appear in contracts/trade-api.yaml, the Angular UI generates its types from that file in Sprint 9, and the database stores the same strings. A renamed or extra literal is a break in three places at once. \\ * There is no partial-fill literal, which is why the Trade Executor fills in full or rejects. \\ * The harness reads compiled classes with javap rather than your source, so a literal commented out or spelled differently in two places is caught rather than matched.

Summary: The Order Request DTO with Validation
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * PlaceOrderRequest carries the six fields in contracts/trade-api.yaml and every constraint on them is enforced and tested. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Constrain the account key to the numeric account identifier, at least 1, and require it. \\ Constrain the symbol to a non-blank value within the contract's length limit. \\ Constrain the side to one of BUY or SELL. \\ Constrain the quantity to whole units greater than zero, which is business rule 4. \\ Constrain the price to greater than zero with at most two decimal places, which is business rule 5. \\ Constrain the idempotency key to the length range in the contract. \\ Keep the DTO in the domain, because those are business constraints rather than transport constraints. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a valid request passes every constraint \\ # a null required field is refused \\ # a non-positive quantity is refused \\ # a non-positive price is refused \\ # a price with three decimal places is refused \\ # an idempotency key either side of the length limits \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Bean Validation annotations are the one framework the architecture allows inside the domain, and jakarta.validation-api is the only compile dependency in the scaffold. Validating by hand is allowed: what is assessed is that every constraint is enforced and tested.

Summary: The Exception Hierarchy
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Six exception types cover account not found, account not active, instrument not found, insufficient funds, insufficient holdings and duplicate order, and all six descend from one domain base type. \\ * The base type carries the catalogue code, not an HTTP status. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Map each case to its code from contracts/trade-api.yaml: ACC-404, ACC-403, INS-404, ORD-400, ORD-409 for insufficient holdings and ORD-409 for a duplicate order. \\ Keep the message to the catalogue message and nothing else: no account key, no symbol, no amount, no class name, no SQL fragment. \\ Carry the values an investigation needs as typed fields on the exception, to be logged on the server. \\ Decide what your hierarchy does about a quantity or price that is out of range, since VAL-422 is a documented outcome with no member in the list of six, and be ready to defend it. \\ Declare the six class names in manifest.env. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * One code can mean two things and one case can carry two codes. An unknown instrument and a suspended instrument both answer INS-404. Neither is an accident. \\ * Put a status on the exception and you have dragged the web layer into the domain a sprint early. Sprint 6 maps a code to a status in one place, and Sprint 7 maps the same code to a rejection reason on a Kafka event.

Summary: Business Rules 1 to 8, in Evaluation Order
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * All eight rules are implemented in the domain and not in a controller, and the first failure wins with no later rule evaluated. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Enforce rule 1, the account must exist, then rule 2, the account must be ACTIVE, then rule 3, the instrument must exist and be tradable. \\ Enforce rules 4 and 5 in the domain as well as on the DTO, because the domain has to hold for a caller that never ran a validator. \\ Enforce rule 6 on a BUY, the cash balance at least quantity multiplied by price, and rule 7 on a SELL, the held quantity at least the order quantity. \\ Enforce rule 8, the idempotency key must not already have been used, and design the seam that lets it be testable here without a database. \\ Leave room for rule 9, cash and position move together or neither moves, and rule 10, every order is recorded including a rejected one. \\ Test the evaluation order itself, not only the eight rules. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # each of the eight rules firing, as an isolated test \\ # each of the eight rules not firing, as an isolated test \\ # a suspended account holding no cash answers ACC-403 and not ORD-400 \\ # a domain object is not half mutated when a precondition fails \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The order is part of the contract. The Angular order ticket branches on the code in Sprint 9. \\ * Rule 8's authority in Sprint 6 is the unique constraint you built in Sprint 3, not a read followed by a write. Two concurrent requests carrying the same key both pass a read-then-write check, and the side effect of losing that race is a duplicated trade.

Summary: Test-First Development and the Three Named Classes
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * AccountTest, OrderLogicTest and PlaceOrderRequestValidationTest exist by those names, are green, and carry at least 24 tests between them. \\ * The commit history shows the tests arriving before the implementation. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Commit a failing test on its own, with a message saying what it asserts, then the smallest implementation that turns it green, then a refactor where there is one. \\ Cover status, debit, credit, affordability, the refusal to go negative and money that does not drift over many operations in AccountTest. \\ Cover the eight rules firing and not firing, plus the evaluation order, in OrderLogicTest. \\ Cover every DTO constraint, including the boundary either side of each limit, in PlaceOrderRequestValidationTest. \\ Commit small, commit often and push as you go, so the history exists somewhere other than one laptop. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A history in which the test for a rule and the implementation of that rule first appear in the same commit does not pass, and a single commit at the end of the week holding the whole module fails outright. \\ * The named classes are a floor, not a target. Write the other classes your entities need.

Summary: A Domain Module with No Framework on its Classpath
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * mvn dependency:tree contains no Spring, servlet or JDBC artefact, including transitively, and sprint-05-domain-engine/scripts/check.sh passes from a clean state. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Leave the banned-dependencies rule in pom.xml in place. It is the criterion enforced by the build rather than by good intentions. \\ Fill in manifest.env with your base package and your six exception class names. \\ Run mvn install so the Sprint 6 service can resolve this module from your local Maven repository by its coordinates. \\ Run scripts/check.sh and fix what it names until clean. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * If you find yourself wanting to remove the rule, the thing you are about to add belongs in Sprint 6. \\ * There is no aggregator build. An install here has to happen before a package in Sprint 6, and again whenever the domain changes. \\ * The harness counts tests, it does not read them. Whether each rule is correct, in the right order and in the domain rather than in a caller is assessed at the review.

Summary: Trade REST API (Spring Boot)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A layered, Dockerised Spring Boot service implements contracts/trade-api.yaml over MyBatis against the Sprint 3 schema, calling the Sprint 5 domain for every rule. \\ * Every route under /api/v1/ verifies a JWT issued by the provided Node auth stub, and rejects a missing or invalid token with AUTH-401. \\ * Order placement is transactional and the account version column carries an optimistic lock. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The contract is the specification. It was written before the service existed so that the Angular application in Sprint 9 can generate a typed client from it without anyone reading your Java. \\ * services/auth-stub is provided. It is a fixture, not a deliverable: nothing in it is assessed and nothing in it is to be modified. It exists because Sprint 6 has to verify a real token and Node is not taught until Sprint 8. Start it with docker compose --profile platform up -d --build. \\ * In Sprint 6 there is no Trade Executor, so POST /api/v1/orders fills synchronously and answers FILLED or REJECTED. From Sprint 7 the same endpoint answers NEW. The contract documents both. \\ * Security focus: token verification before any controller runs, Bean Validation on request DTOs, and an error envelope that leaks nothing (OWASP A01, A03, A05). \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-06-trade-api/scripts/check.sh and of scripts/check.sh --live.

Summary: Project Setup and the Layered Structure
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Controller, service and mapper layers exist with clear responsibilities, and no SQL appears in a controller and no HTTP type in the domain. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Add web, validation, MyBatis, the Postgres driver and the OpenAPI dependencies, and resolve the Sprint 5 domain module by its coordinates. \\ Keep the coordinates in agreement across sprint-05-domain-engine/pom.xml, the domain properties in this pom.xml, and manifest.env. \\ Let the controller speak HTTP, DTOs, status codes and validation annotations only. \\ Let the service speak the domain module, the mappers and one transaction, and never take a servlet type, a request object or a status code as a parameter. \\ Let the mapper speak parameterised SQL and result mapping, and decide nothing. \\ Read every value that differs between a laptop and a container from an environment variable, with a default that works under Docker Compose. Commit no secret, including the development ones. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A query written in the class that handles the request cannot be tested without a web layer and cannot be reused by the service that needs the same rows next sprint. \\ * The domain module must still build with no servlet API and no Spring on its classpath. The Trade Executor in Sprint 7 is the second caller and it has no HTTP request.

Summary: The Six Endpoints Against the Contract
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * POST /api/v1/orders, DELETE /api/v1/orders/{id}, GET /api/v1/accounts/{id}, /balance, /positions and /orders are implemented and match contracts/trade-api.yaml field for field. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Implement order placement and cancellation, returning the recorded order and the cancelled order in the contract's shapes. \\ Implement the four account reads, with positions limited to a net quantity above zero and order history newest first. \\ Match AccountResponse carefully: it is the one place in the platform where accountId means the string business reference, and AccountResponse.id is what every other endpoint calls accountId. \\ Return ORD-409 when cancelling an order that cannot be cancelled. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # an order is placed and answers the contract shape \\ # an order is refused on a business-rule failure and answers the documented code \\ # a working order is cancelled successfully \\ # cancelling a filled or already cancelled order answers ORD-409 \\ # account, balance, positions and order history each answer for a valid account \\ # an unknown account answers ACC-404 \\  \\ *Integration Test* \\  \\ Place and cancel an order through the real controller, service and MyBatis persistence against Postgres, then read the account, balance, positions and order history back. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Getting AccountResponse wrong compiles, passes your own tests, and breaks the generated client in Sprint 9.

Summary: MyBatis Mappers with Parameterised Statements
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Every value arriving from outside the service is bound with #{}, and no ${} appears in any mapper statement, XML or annotation. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Write mapper interfaces in Java and statements in XML under src/main/resources/mapper/, or in annotations on the interface. \\ Bind the account key, the symbol, the status filter and every timestamp as parameters. \\ Return the affected row count from any mapper that updates, because a mapper returning void has thrown away the only evidence that anything happened. \\ If you need an interpolated column name or sort direction, check the value against a fixed list of permitted names first and declare the file and the token in MAPPER_SQL_INTERPOLATION_ALLOWLIST in manifest.env. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # an order row is inserted and read back \\ # an account and its positions read correctly \\ # a constraint violation surfaces rather than being swallowed \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * ${} is a string substitution performed before the statement reaches the driver. A symbol crafted by an attacker becomes part of the statement, and the account whose positions come back is whichever account they asked for. That is OWASP A03. \\ * The allowlist ships empty, and an entry in it is a question you will be asked in the review.

Summary: Transactional Order Placement
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Order placement is annotated @Transactional so that the order record, the cash movement and the position write succeed or fail together. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Put the transaction boundary around the work that has to be atomic, and nothing more. \\ Call the Sprint 5 domain for every rule. The service owns transport and persistence, not the decision. \\ Record the order whatever the outcome, including a rejection, because the order table is the audit trail. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a placed order commits the cash movement and the position together \\ # a failed order rolls back with no partial write \\ # a rejected order is still recorded

Summary: Optimistic Locking on the Account Version
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Every write to the account row names the version it was read at and increments it, and zero rows affected is treated as the refusal it is. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read the version with the row rather than fetching it separately. \\ Make the update conditional on that version, and answer ORD-409 when it affects no rows. \\ Apply the same reasoning to the order state transition behind DELETE /api/v1/orders/{id}: make the transition conditional on the state you expect, in one statement. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a concurrent update is detected and the second write affects no rows \\ # a lost update surfaces as a refusal rather than as a silently wrong balance \\ # cancelling an order that is no longer NEW affects no rows and answers ORD-409 \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Without the lock, two buys of 20,000 against a balance of 25,000 both succeed and the account is left with 5,000 instead of being 15,000 overdrawn. There is no error, no log line and no symptom until somebody reconciles cash against the order history the next morning.

Summary: Global Exception Handler and the Error Catalogue
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * One @ControllerAdvice maps every domain exception to its documented code and status, and every failure leaves the service as the error envelope and nothing else. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Return {"errorCode": ..., "message": ...} for every failure. Not a whitelabel page, not a stack trace, not a bare status with an empty body. \\ Map ACC-404 to 404, ACC-403 to 403, INS-404 to 404, ORD-400 to 400, ORD-409 to 409, VAL-422 to 422 and AUTH-401 to 401. \\ Keep the message free of class names, SQL fragments, account keys and internal identifiers, and log those on the server instead. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # account not found maps to ACC-404 with status 404 \\ # an inactive account maps to ACC-403 with status 403 \\ # insufficient funds maps to ORD-400 with status 400 \\ # insufficient holdings and a reused idempotency key both map to ORD-409 \\ # a field validation failure maps to VAL-422 with status 422 \\ # no response body carries a stack trace or an internal identifier \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The Angular application has one error handler because there is one envelope. Clients branch on errorCode and never on the status alone, because 404 and 409 each carry more than one code.

Summary: JWT Verification Against the Provided Auth Stub
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Every route under /api/v1/ verifies the token before any controller runs, and a missing, malformed, expired or wrongly signed token answers AUTH-401 with the same body in all four cases. \\ * A caller whose accountId claim does not reach the account in the request answers ACC-403, with the same message a suspended account gets. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read services/auth-stub/README.md for the demo users, the claims the token carries and the shared signing secret. \\ Check the signature, the expiry and the algorithm the token asks for, in that order, before reading a single claim. \\ Read the signing secret from JWT_SECRET in the environment, never from a properties file. \\ Answer authentication once for every protected route, and answer authorisation where the account key is known. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a valid token from the stub is accepted \\ # a missing Authorization header answers AUTH-401 \\ # a wrong scheme answers AUTH-401 \\ # an expired token answers AUTH-401 \\ # a forged signature answers AUTH-401 \\ # a token whose accountId claim does not reach the account answers ACC-403 \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The stub is a fixture. It has no tests to write and nothing in it is assessed. \\ * A verifier that decodes the payload first and checks the signature afterwards has already trusted whatever the client sent. \\ * A more specific message tells an attacker which of the four they got wrong, which is a free oracle and costs you nothing to avoid. \\ * Sprint 8 replaces the stub with the real service. The claims, the algorithm and the secret are identical by design, so the swap is a configuration change and no code in this service is expected to change.

Summary: Structured Logging
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The service emits structured logs sufficient to audit order activity, and no secret or sensitive payload reaches them. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Log order placement, cancellation and every mapped error, with the values an investigation needs. \\ Keep tokens, secrets and request bodies out of the log calls.

Summary: Multi-Stage Dockerfile and the Compose Entry
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The service builds and runs from a multi-stage Dockerfile whose final stage is not a build image, and it starts under docker compose --profile platform. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read Dockerfile.example, which is the naive single-stage version, then write Dockerfile properly. \\ Build in one stage that has Maven and a JDK 21, and run from a separate stage that has neither, copying the built jar across. \\ Run as a user that is not root, expose the service port and answer a health check. \\ Order the copies so a change to a source file does not invalidate the layer holding the resolved dependencies. \\ Set the build context so it contains both this folder and sprint-05-domain-engine, because the image build cannot see the Maven repository on your laptop. \\ Add the service to docker-compose.yml with a build block, profiles [platform], networks [trading-net], a published port, the database variables, JWT_SECRET passed through from .env, depends_on Postgres on its health condition, and a health check. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * localhost inside a container is the container. The compose service name is postgres. \\ * Nothing in this sprint needs Kafka. The broker starts with the infrastructure and this service ignores it until Sprint 7.

Summary: Event Backbone: Kafka, the Trade Executor and the Batch Pipeline
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Three topics carry the platform's events with the keys, partition counts and retention in contracts/kafka-topics.md. \\ * The Trade REST API publishes accepted orders to orders and answers NEW. The team builds the Trade Executor, which consumes orders, prices against a live Fauxnance quote, applies fill or reject rules, updates order, cash and position in one transaction, and publishes to trade-events. \\ * The team builds the market-data poller that creates the price stream, and a batch pipeline that loads FACT_TRADES with dead-letter handling. \\ * Characterisation tests are written before any refactoring of the provided starter, and the SonarQube gate passes on the Java services and the pipeline. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * There is no broker simulator in this platform and there will not be one. You build the execution venue, and it is the only component that decides whether an order fills. \\ * Fauxnance has no stream. The poller is what manufactures it, and its existence is the reason the Sprint 10 extensions that read prices have anything to consume. The quota is 2000 requests per day per key, shared between the poller and the executor. \\ * Kafka guarantees at-least-once, deliberately, because the alternative is a broker that occasionally loses a trade. The deliverable is not a consumer that works, it is a consumer that is correct when the message arrives twice, and a team that can prove it on demand. \\ * Security focus: DevSecOps in CI with SAST, dependency scanning and secret detection, and SonarQube quality gates (OWASP A06, A08). \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-07-event-backbone/scripts/check.sh and of scripts/check.sh --live.

Summary: Three Topics with Documented Keys and Partition Counts
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * orders, trade-events and market-data exist with the keys, partition counts and retention the contract fixes, and the team can defend the key and partition choices. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Create orders keyed by the account, with 3 partitions and 7-day retention, as a work queue with exactly one consumer group. \\ Create trade-events keyed by the account, with 3 partitions and 30-day retention, as the platform's event log. \\ Create market-data keyed by symbol, with 6 partitions and 1-day retention. \\ Create the three dead-letter topics named <topic>.DLT, alongside them. \\ Create topics explicitly through infra/kafka/create-topics.sh rather than relying on auto-creation. \\ Record the reasoning for the key and the partition count where your team keeps its decisions. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Kafka orders messages within a partition and promises nothing across partitions. Keying by account is what stops a sell being processed before the buy that made it possible. Keying by order identifier puts every message on its own partition and throws the guarantee away. \\ * Partitions can be increased and never decreased, and increasing them rehashes the keys. \\ * Serialisation is JSON, one envelope on all three topics, and consumers ignore fields they do not recognise.

Summary: Publish to orders and Answer NEW
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * POST /api/v1/orders writes the order at NEW, answers NEW, and publishes an ORDER_PLACED message to orders keyed by the account after the transaction commits. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Stop computing a fill in the Sprint 6 service. There is no price in that request and pricing is the executor's job. \\ Publish after the commit, never inside the transaction. \\ Configure the producer with acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, a high retry count and no more than five requests in flight per connection. \\ Leave the validation, the layering, the error catalogue, the optimistic lock and the token verification exactly as they are. \\ Expect your Sprint 6 live checks that asserted a terminal status to see NEW, which is correct. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # the order is persisted and then the event is published \\ # a rolled-back order publishes no event \\ # a publish failure leaves a committed order that can be recovered by replay \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Publishing inside the transaction risks an event for an order that then rolled back, and nothing can undo that. Publishing after risks an order that committed and was never published, and that is recoverable by replaying from the order table. Choose the recoverable failure. \\ * An idempotent producer removes the duplicates a producer retry causes. It does not remove the duplicates an application retry causes, which is why the executor still has work to do.

Summary: Build the Trade Executor Consumer
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A separate deployable consumes orders in the consumer group trade-executor, and settles, publishes and acknowledges in that order. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Build the executor under executor/ as its own service, subscribed to orders with an explicit group.id of trade-executor. \\ Load the order from Postgres on receipt, and treat a status other than NEW as a previous delivery having already settled it. \\ Check the instrument is still tradable before fetching a price. \\ Settle in one transaction, then publish to trade-events, then acknowledge the offset. \\ Handle partition rebalancing. \\ Add the executor to docker-compose.yml under the platform profile, with KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS pointing at kafka:29092, FAUXNANCE_API_KEY passed through from .env, the database variables and depends_on Postgres on its health condition. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a message is consumed and the offset committed after processing \\ # an order already in a terminal status is recognised and nothing is written \\ # a rebalance reassigns partitions without losing a message \\ # more consumers than partitions leaves one idle \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Publishing before the commit risks an event for a transaction that rolled back. Acknowledging before publishing risks an order that settled in Postgres and told nobody.

Summary: Fill Pricing Against a Live Quote and Settlement in One Transaction
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Each order is priced against a live Fauxnance quote, the fill or reject rule is applied, and the order status, the cash movement and the position write happen in one transaction or not at all. \\ * ORDER_FILLED or ORDER_REJECTED is published to trade-events, keyed by the account. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Fetch a quote with GET /quotes/{symbol}, reading the key from FAUXNANCE_API_KEY. \\ Start from the workable default: fill the whole order at the quoted price when a BUY limit price is at or above the quote or a SELL limit price is at or below it, and reject otherwise. The rule is your design decision, constrained by business rules 1 to 8. \\ Write the rule as a function of an order and a quote returning a decision. It touches no database and no socket, which is the only reason its interesting cases will get tested. \\ Decide and defend four details: what price is stored and when you round, which of the Sprint 5 rules are re-checked here, what a suspended account does when it was suspended after acceptance, and what happens when no price can be obtained. \\ Add a migration for the columns the executor writes that your Sprint 3 schema may not have yet: the price a fill happened at, when it happened, and why an order was rejected. \\ Apply the optimistic lock on the account version inside the transaction, re-reading and retrying up to a bounded number of attempts. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a marketable buy fills at the quoted price and debits cash once \\ # a non-marketable order is rejected with a stated reason \\ # a buy is rejected when cash no longer covers it at execution time \\ # a sell is rejected when holdings no longer cover it at execution time \\ # an account suspended after acceptance does not trade \\ # no quote available produces a rejection rather than an order left at NEW \\ # a rejection is published to trade-events rather than swallowed \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Partial fills are out of scope, because OrderStatus has no state to represent one. There is no working state between NEW and a terminal status, so an unmarketable order is rejected rather than rested. \\ * An order marked filled beside cash that did not move leaves the audit trail disagreeing with the balance, and nothing in the platform reconciles the two for you. \\ * A price feed being down is a business outcome, not a message-processing failure. Leaving the order at NEW for ever is worse than rejecting it.

Summary: Idempotent Processing, Retries and Dead-Letter Routing
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Replaying a duplicate message does not double-debit an account, no second event appears on trade-events, and the team can demonstrate that live at any point in the review. \\ * A poison message is dead-lettered on the first attempt and a transient failure is retried with a growing backoff before it is dead-lettered. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Make the guarded state transition the first write in the transaction, conditioned on the status you expect, and treat zero rows affected as another delivery having got there first. \\ Dead-letter on the first attempt anything that will never succeed: malformed JSON, a missing order identifier, an order identifier not in Postgres, an unexpected event type. \\ Retry with backoff anything that will succeed later: a briefly unreachable broker, a lost database connection, an exhausted optimistic-lock budget. Dead-letter once the budget is spent. \\ Do not retry a poison message indefinitely. One bad message blocking a partition stops every account keyed to that partition. \\ Rehearse the demonstration: read one message off orders, produce it back, then show the balance before, the balance after, the log line where the executor recognised the duplicate, and the absence of a second event on trade-events. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a duplicate delivery leaves cash and position unchanged \\ # a duplicate delivery publishes no second event \\ # a malformed message is dead-lettered on the first attempt \\ # a transient failure is retried with backoff and then succeeds \\ # an exhausted retry budget dead-letters rather than looping \\  \\ *Integration Test* \\  \\ Run scripts/check.sh --live, which places an order, produces the message back onto orders, and asserts that the balance did not move and no second event appeared. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Being able to run the script is not the same as being able to give the demonstration, and the review asks for the demonstration. \\ * A read, then a decision, then a write can be run twice by two deliveries. A write conditioned on the state it expects cannot, because the database serialises the two updates.

Summary: Market-Data Poller
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A poller calls the batch quotes endpoint on an interval and publishes one message per symbol to market-data, keyed by symbol. \\ * It batches up to 25 symbols per call and stays inside the daily quota, and the arithmetic behind the chosen interval is written down. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Call GET /quotes?symbols=A,B,C with at most 25 symbols, which costs one request whatever the symbol count. \\ Publish one message per symbol, never one per batch, because batching the Kafka message puts several symbols behind one key and destroys the per-symbol ordering the contract promises. \\ Poll only the symbols you hold or watch. \\ Enforce a floor on the interval in code rather than documenting one and hoping. \\ Give the poller a budget that is its share of the quota rather than the whole of it, because the executor needs quotes to price fills. \\ Add the poller to docker-compose.yml under the platform profile, with the bootstrap servers and the Fauxnance key from the environment. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a batch of 25 symbols is one Fauxnance request \\ # one Kafka message is published per symbol \\ # polling is limited to held and watched symbols \\ # the interval floor cannot be configured below its limit \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Eight symbols fetched one at a time every 30 seconds is 23040 requests and the key is gone in a little over two hours. The same data batched is 2880. \\ * Nothing at a 30 second interval survives being left running overnight. Stop the container at the end of the session, or run at 60 seconds. \\ * The Angular application never calls Fauxnance, because that ships a key to every browser that loads the page.

Summary: Batch Pipeline into the Analytical Store
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The pipeline loads FACT_TRADES and its three dimensions from Postgres, incrementally and idempotently, with dead-letter handling for bad rows. \\ * The post-load reconciliation agrees with Postgres on row count and summed trade value for a day. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Load dimensions before facts: dim_date across the whole range, then dim_instrument, then dim_account, then fact_trades. \\ Drive the load from a watermark on the order creation timestamp so a scheduled run reads what is new rather than the whole table. \\ Merge on the natural key rather than inserting, so re-running yesterday's load does not double-count. \\ Load rejected and cancelled orders as well as fills, because fill rate cannot be computed from fills alone. The grain is one order in whatever status it reached. \\ Run every check in the contract's load and data quality section before a row reaches the fact table: referential integrity into all three dimensions, positive quantity and price, a valid side and status, and a trade value recomputed rather than trusted. \\ Send a failing row somewhere with the reason it failed and the batch it came from. \\ Reconcile the fact table against Postgres after the load. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a first load populates the dimensions and the fact table \\ # a second load with no new data adds no rows \\ # a row failing a quality check reaches the dead-letter path and not the fact table \\ # the pipeline continues after a bad row \\ # a transient failure is retried and then succeeds \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Do not insert a placeholder dimension row to make an unresolved key pass. That hides the fault, which is almost always that the dimension load was skipped. \\ * Dropping a row silently and dead-lettering it produce the same fact table, and only one of them can be investigated on Monday morning.

Summary: Characterisation Tests Before Refactoring the Starter
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Characterisation tests exist under etl-starter/tests/ and pass, and the first commit that adds one is an ancestor of the first commit after the scaffold that touches etl-starter/src/. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Run the provided loader against the seeded stack first and read what it does. etl-starter/README.md says how. \\ Write tests that record what the loader does now, including the parts you disagree with, so that a change altering behaviour by accident fails loudly instead of quietly. \\ Start where the behaviour is observable: what warehouse a known set of source rows produces, what happens to a row that cannot be placed, what a second run does to a warehouse that already holds the first. \\ Use etl-starter/fixtures/source-rows.json so a test can put rows through the loader without a Postgres container. \\ Then refactor: separate what does not belong together, make the load idempotent, give bad rows somewhere to go, and keep the tests green while you do it. \\ Where you decide a behaviour was wrong and change it deliberately, change the test in the same commit and say so in the message. \\ Commit in small pieces. A history of one commit per week cannot show this. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The starter is flawed by design. Somebody wrote it under pressure, it went into service, and it has been running ever since. The list of flaws is not published, it is not in this repository and you will not be given it. Finding them is the exercise. \\ * You cannot write a characterisation test after the change, because a test written against refactored code records the behaviour of the refactored code, which is the one thing it cannot then be used to check. \\ * Tests and a change to the loader in the same commit do not satisfy the rule. Neither does tidying the loader first and pinning it afterwards.

Summary: SonarQube Quality Gate and DevSecOps Scanning
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The default quality gate passes on the Java services and on the pipeline, with no new blocker or critical issue and no new security hotspot left unreviewed. \\ * SAST, dependency scanning and secret detection run locally against the same code, and anything they report is fixed rather than left for the review. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Run SonarQube locally in a container named for your team, create a project and generate a token. Export the token, never commit it. \\ Scan the Java services with the Maven scanner and the Python pipeline with the scanner image. \\ Act on the findings during the week rather than on Friday. \\ Run SAST and dependency scanning as part of the local scan, and secret detection from scripts/check.sh, and fix what they report during the week. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * scripts/check.sh does not run SonarQube. The gate is checked at the review, on your screen, on the project you scanned. \\ * Passing by marking findings as will not fix is visible in the dashboard and is not passing.

Summary: Dashboard Reading Both Sources
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The Sprint 4 dashboard reads from both the real-time stream and the batch analytical store, and the two views are reconciled. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Extend the Sprint 4 dashboard to read the loaded star schema as well as the market-data stream. \\ Reconcile the two views and explain any discrepancy rather than hiding it.

Summary: Authentication Service (NestJS)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A NestJS service implements contracts/auth-api.yaml: register, login, refresh and a protected current-user route, with credentials hashed in Postgres. \\ * The access token carries exactly the claims contract, refresh tokens rotate, and a failed login answers identically for an unknown user and a wrong password. \\ * Swapping the provided stub for this service is a configuration change only, with no code change in the Trade REST API. \\ * The running service serves its own OpenAPI document, and an OWASP security review is committed with a finding and a disposition in every category. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * This is the one component that ever sees a credential. Every other component verifies a signature with no network call and no shared database. \\ * services/auth-stub has been standing in since Sprint 6. It has no database, no registration, no hashing and no refresh. This sprint retires it. \\ * Security focus: password hashing, token issuance and lifecycle, replay and timing attacks, and access control on the current-user route (OWASP A01, A02, A04, A07). \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-08-auth-service/scripts/check.sh and of scripts/check.sh --live.

Summary: NestJS Scaffold, Module Structure and the Dockerfile
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A modular, layered TypeScript service builds from the files in the repository, installs from the lock file, and runs from a multi-stage Dockerfile you wrote. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Organise the modules so each has a single responsibility and a dependency direction it respects, and tell the harness what you chose in manifest.env. \\ Commit package-lock.json, because a build that resolves a different tree on a teammate's laptop is not the build you tested. \\ Write the Dockerfile: build in a stage that has the toolchain, run in a stage that does not, copy the artefact across, run as a user that is not root, expose the port and answer a health check. \\ Install production dependencies deliberately rather than copying a development tree across. \\ Copy .env.example to .env and take JWT_SECRET from the repository root .env. It ships empty on purpose. \\ Replace the auth-stub entry in docker-compose.yml with your service, on the same port. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * There is no Dockerfile in this folder deliberately. You wrote one for a Spring Boot service in Sprint 6 and writing the equivalent for a Node service is the exercise. \\ * If you chose argon2, it is a native module: the build stage needs a compiler, the runtime stage must not have one, and the binding has to be built against the same Node version and platform the runtime stage uses.

Summary: The Four Endpoints Against the Contract
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * POST /auth/register, POST /auth/login, POST /auth/refresh and GET /auth/me are implemented and match contracts/auth-api.yaml, including the error envelope and every code in it. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Return 201 and a user response from registration, and issue no tokens from it. \\ Refuse a registration naming a trading account that does not exist, because accounts are owned by the Sprint 3 schema. \\ Return 200 and a token response from login and from refresh. \\ Protect /auth/me with a bearer token and read the identity from the verified token, never from a parameter the client controls. \\ Validate inputs with class-validator and return VAL-422 where the contract says so, and AUTH-409 for a username already taken. \\ Use the platform envelope, {"errorCode": ..., "message": ...} and nothing else. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # registration succeeds for a new user and issues no token \\ # registration for an existing username answers AUTH-409 \\ # registration naming an unknown account fails validation \\ # login succeeds and returns a token pair \\ # refresh returns a new pair for a valid refresh token \\ # /auth/me answers from the verified token and not from a request parameter \\  \\ *Integration Test* \\  \\ Exercise register, login, refresh and /auth/me against the running service and its Postgres store. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * An unauthenticated route that mints a session is an authentication bypass as soon as it has its first defect, so the client logs in afterwards. \\ * AUTH-409 extends the catalogue and is scoped to this service, because registration is not a trading operation.

Summary: Password Storage and Never Logging a Credential
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Passwords are stored with argon2id, or with bcrypt at cost 12 or above, and a plaintext password never reaches a log or a repository. \\ * The cost factors are a decision the team can defend. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Choose parameters that make one verification take on the order of a tenth of a second on the hardware you deploy to, and write down what you chose and why. \\ Never use MD5, SHA-256 or an unsalted digest of any kind. \\ Log through one logger that redacts by key name at any depth, so a nested object cannot smuggle a field past you. \\ Never pass a whole request body to a log call. Pass the fields you actually want instead. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a correct password verifies \\ # an incorrect password fails verification \\ # a plaintext password never reaches the repository layer \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A general-purpose hash is built to be fast, and fast is the one property a password hash must not have. A stolen table of SHA-256 digests is a stolen table of passwords by the weekend. \\ * Too low a cost and an offline attacker gets the same speedup you did. Too high and your login route becomes the cheapest denial-of-service target in the platform. \\ * The harness catches a log call that names a credential field. The indirect routes, an error object serialised whole or a stack trace, are what the review asks about.

Summary: Access Token Issuance with Exactly the Claims Contract
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The access token carries sub, accountId, roles, iat and exp, plus the iss the contract also defines, and nothing else. \\ * It is signed HS256 with the secret in JWT_SECRET and expires fifteen minutes after issue. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Carry sub as the stable user identifier and not the username, because a username can change. \\ Carry accountId as the numeric trading account key, which the Trade REST API compares against the account in the request. \\ Carry roles as a non-empty array of CUSTOMER or ADMIN. \\ Set iss to auth-service, so that during the cutover a team can decode a token and see which implementation signed it. Consumers must not require a particular value for it. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a token is issued with exactly the contractual claims \\ # the expiry is fifteen minutes after the issued-at time \\ # the signature verifies with the service key \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Anything beyond those six claims is a finding, not a bonus. The payload is base64 and not encryption: paste one into any decoder and read it. \\ * Removing a claim after Sprint 9 has generated a client from it is not a configuration change.

Summary: Refresh Rotation and Reuse Detection
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A refresh rotates the refresh token itself, the presented token stops working at that instant, and presenting a consumed token revokes every live refresh token for that user and answers AUTH-401. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Store a hash of the refresh token rather than the token, so that read access to your database is not session takeover. \\ Make the consumption conditional in the statement that performs it, the way Sprint 6 made the account update conditional on the version. \\ Kill the old value in your store before the response is written. \\ Treat a second presentation as theft, because the service cannot tell a repeated client request from a stolen token. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a refresh issues a new pair and the old refresh token stops working \\ # a consumed refresh token presented again answers AUTH-401 \\ # reuse revokes the whole chain for that user \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * An access token cannot be withdrawn. It is verified by signature alone, and fifteen minutes is the size of that compromise. The refresh token is the opposite: opaque, stored and revocable. \\ * Without rotation a thief holds a seven-day credential and uses it quietly, and the real user notices nothing because their own token still works.

Summary: One Answer for Every Failure
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * An unknown username and a wrong password answer with the same status, the same body and comparable timing. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Answer AUTH-401 with the same message for an unknown user, a wrong password, an expired token, a wrongly signed token, a consumed refresh token and a malformed header. \\ Answer 401 for all of them. A 404 for an unknown user and a 401 for a bad password is the same disclosure written in the status line. \\ Where the username is not found, verify the supplied password against a fixed dummy hash of the same algorithm and the same parameters, discard the result and return the same failure. \\ Build a throttle on the login route, and declare THROTTLE_COOLDOWN_SECONDS and UNIFORM_TIMING_ATTEMPTS in manifest.env so the harness waits out your window. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # an unknown user and a wrong password produce identical status and body \\ # both paths perform one password verification \\ # a throttled request is refused without leaking which credential was wrong \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * If the unknown-user path returns as soon as the lookup misses, it answers in a millisecond while the wrong-password path spends a tenth of a second verifying a hash. An attacker with a username list and a stopwatch reads your customer base off the response times. \\ * Throttling is not a substitute for the uniform failure. It limits how fast an attacker can use an oracle you left open, rather than closing it.

Summary: The Guard and its Two Named Jest Paths
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Jest covers the guard, including a passing test for the expired-token path and one for the wrong-signature path, and the suite runs without a database and without an HTTP server. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Build the expired case by signing a genuine token with a past exp, not by corrupting the payload, which the signature check would catch first. \\ Build the wrong-signature case by signing a genuine, unexpired token with a different key. \\ Verify the signature before any claim is read. \\ Name the tests however you like and correct the patterns in manifest.env if your names do not match the defaults. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a valid token is accepted \\ # a token with an exp in the past is refused \\ # a well-formed token with a wrong signature is refused before a claim is read \\ # a malformed token is refused \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A guard that checks the signature and forgets the clock accepts every token it ever issued, forever. \\ * Expect to be asked at the review for tests covering the identical failure for an unknown user and a wrong password, rotation and replay, and the fact that a plaintext password never reaches your repository.

Summary: OpenAPI Served by the Running Service
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The running service publishes its own OpenAPI document, describing all four routes, at the paths declared in manifest.env. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Generate the document from the decorators on your controller and DTOs and serve it from the process. \\ Declare the human page and the JSON document paths in manifest.env. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A YAML file maintained by hand beside the code drifts from the code within a fortnight. The document that matters is the one describing what is deployed. \\ * The generated document is not a replacement for contracts/auth-api.yaml, which remains the source of truth binding both implementations. It is the evidence that your code still matches it.

Summary: Retire the Stub by Configuration Only
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A token from this service is accepted by a protected Trade REST API route with no Java changed, and the stub is removed from docker-compose.yml. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Point the compose service that answers on the auth port at your service and remove the auth-stub service. \\ Read the same JWT_SECRET the Trade REST API verifies with. \\ Where the Trade REST API pins an issuer, move that setting to your issuer through the environment. \\ Configure the database connection for the credential store. \\ Write the parity check the stub's README asks for: sign with both implementations and cross-verify the claim names, types, algorithm and lifetime. \\ Decide whether to keep or rotate the stub's published development secret, and declare the decision in manifest.env under STUB_SECRET_EXPECTATION. \\ Bring the git diff to the review showing no Java changed. \\  \\ *Integration Test* \\  \\ Obtain a token from your service, call a protected Trade REST API route with it, then repeat with a token signed by a key the platform should not trust and confirm it is refused. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Not a small code change, and not only a configuration class: no Java changes. If yours needs one, something in the Trade REST API is coupled to the fixture rather than to the token. The usual culprits are a hard-coded issuer string, a claim read with a name the stub happened to use, and a verifier that decoded before it verified. \\ * The stub's development secret is published in its own README, so anyone who has read this repository can mint a token your consumers accept for as long as that secret is in use.

Summary: OWASP Security Review of the Auth Flow
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A security review is committed in security-review/, differs from the template, and carries a written finding and a written disposition for every category. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Copy security-review/TEMPLATE.md to a file of your own, name it in manifest.env, and fill it in as you build rather than the night before. \\ Cover A01 broken access control, A02 cryptographic failures, A03 injection, A04 insecure design, A05 security misconfiguration, A06 vulnerable and outdated components, A07 identification and authentication failures, and A09 security logging and monitoring failures. \\ Where the finding is none, justify it in a sentence naming what you checked. \\ Where the disposition is accepted, say what the residual risk is and why the team is carrying it. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * None with nothing beside it is indistinguishable from a category nobody looked at. \\ * The harness checks that every category has both cells filled. Whether the sentence is true is read by your instructor.

Summary: Trading UI (Angular)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The Angular application signs in against the real Auth service and delivers the dashboard, the order ticket and the blotter. \\ * Its API clients are generated from contracts/ rather than hand-written, one interceptor attaches the bearer token to platform calls and to nothing else, and route guards block and redirect. \\ * Every error code in both catalogues renders as a readable message, Playwright covers three journeys, and no API key or secret is present in the built bundle. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Every API this application consumes already exists and your team wrote all of it. Nothing here is blocked on a service somebody else has to finish. \\ * Execution is asynchronous. The Trade REST API answers before the fill exists. An interface that renders the response to POST /api/v1/orders as the outcome shows NEW and stops, and the team goes looking for a defect in the Trade Executor that is not there. \\ * Standalone components and signals throughout. No NgModules anywhere. \\ * Security focus: the interceptor allow list, guards as a usability control rather than a security control, and a bundle that is public by definition (OWASP A01, A03, A05). \\ * Definition of done includes a clean run of sprint-09-trading-ui/scripts/check.sh and of scripts/check.sh --live.

Summary: Typed Clients Generated from the Contracts
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Both clients are produced by npm run generate from contracts/trade-api.yaml and contracts/auth-api.yaml, committed under src/app/core/api/, and identical to a fresh regeneration. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Run npm run generate, which reads openapitools.json and runs the OpenAPI Generator twice, into the trade and auth client directories. \\ Commit the generated output rather than ignoring it, so a clone builds with no Java runtime and no network and a contract change arrives as a diff a reviewer can read. \\ Regenerate after every contract change and commit the result in the same commit as the code that adapts to it. \\ Never edit a file inside the generated tree, and never reformat it. Wrap an awkward shape in a service of your own under src/app/core/services/. \\ Move the providers out of the placeholder bootstrap into an ApplicationConfig, write a real root component and declare your routes. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * When a contract changes a field, a generated client stops compiling at every call site that used it, and a hand-written one keeps compiling and starts returning undefined at runtime. That is the whole reason the contract exists. \\ * The harness regenerates both clients into a temporary directory and diffs them against yours, and fails if a file appears inside the generated tree that the generator did not write.

Summary: Sign-In Against the Real Auth Service
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A user signs in end to end against the running Auth service, the token is stored, and the session is cleared on sign-out. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Build the login feature with a username field, a password field and a submit button, each carrying a stable data-testid. \\ Show a readable error on a refused sign-in and redirect on success. \\ Keep the two API origins in src/environments/ in step, because a value added to one and not the other is a runtime undefined the compiler cannot see. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # valid credentials sign in and redirect \\ # refused credentials show the readable error rather than the raw message \\ # empty fields are blocked before submission \\ # signing out clears the session \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * The Auth service and the retired stub implement the same contract and both listen on the same port, so pointing this application at one or the other is a change to one line. That is the whole of the no code change criterion from Sprint 8.

Summary: The Bearer Token Interceptor
